fullText:
Alex Gibney’s marathon documentary delivers numerous eye-raising insights into the broligarch’s business deals, early idealism and apocalyptic appetite for fathering children

Veteran documentarian Alex Gibney’s film about the richest broligarch on the planet has been one of the most eagerly anticipated films at the Venice film festival this year. The Oscar-winning 72-year-old, who has in previous films taken on the US military, the Catholic church, Vladimir Putin and Scientology, has been investigating the tech tycoon’s ascent and speaking to people in his orbit since late 2022, before his Maga turn and Trump 2.0.

The result clocks in at just under four hours and presents a comprehensive answer to how on earth one man managed to amass so much money and political influence. It is shocking less for any individual new pieces of information Gibney has unearthed than for its totality. Here are six things the film tells us:

Musk is a genius – at tricking the government into giving him assistance

At Maga rallies, Musk has been introduced as “America’s biggest capitalist”, but Gibney reminds us that he’s always been more than happy to go begging to the state for handouts – such as by cosying up to Obama to gain government contracts for SpaceX to launch satellites for Nasa and the military. The film zooms in on a Tesla press event in June 2013, where Musk unveiled a new “battery swap” system that promised to remove and replace the drained battery pack of a Model S with a fully charged one in just 90 seconds. As it turns out, the technology was never rolled out, and interviewees tell Gibney that a demonstration site at Harris Ranch was barely used for the process. Instead, the film-maker suggests that Musk’s over-promise allowed Tesla to get more ZEV credits from the Californian government, which are awarded to electric car makers based on range and which Musk could then sell to more polluting manufacturers.

In spite of everything, there was something admirable about Musk once

Gibney’s film serves as a reminder that Musk has never been in possession of charm or charisma – the petulant perma-poster retweeting praise is not far from the self-regarding twentysomething start-up bro. But what he did with the funds he earned from selling shares of his first software companies, Zip2, X.com and PayPal, was unusual, Gibney concedes. Where others turned to venture capital, Musk turned to engineering. It’s partially an act, we learn from his ex-wife Justine when she recalls how self-consciously he picked his wardrobe, telling her “I can’t look cool or hip, because I need to look like an engineer”. But in footage of Musk biting his nails with fellow engineers during SpaceX rocket launches his enthusiasm and emotional investment is genuine, and at times infectious.

Musk’s procreation drive is motivated by a fear of civilisational breakdown

Musk has 14 publicly known children, and sources tell Gibney that there are probably more. Some of them were conceived in romantic relationships but more recently the circumstances of their birth seem to have been entirely transactional, via sperm donations to employees of his companies. In a text message to one of his ex-partners, influencer Ashley St Clair, Musk said his desire to have “a legion of children” was driven by a fear of “civil war”. The documentary mostly places the roots of that fear in his South African childhood (in one scene, his father Errol Musk talks with no visible remorse of shooting three intruders in their home). “It’s no doubt he had a traumatic childhood,” Gibney said at a press conference in Venice. “He’s now playing out the trauma on the rest of us.” But, oddly for a man who was long a prominent atheist, the film also hints at a religious dimension to his vision of the apocalypse. The sordid business of negotiating disbursements and NDAs with the mothers of Musk’s children are handled by his right-hand man Jared Birchall, a devout Mormon whom St Clair calls his “henchman” and “demon”.

To Musk, empathy is good in principle but not in action

Recently, Musk has held forth at length about his view that “suicidal empathy” – people who have more empathy for criminals than the victims of criminals, in his view – is behind the decline of western civilisation. Empathy isn’t bad, he says in the doc, it’s just that it’s become too shallow. But interviews in the film raise the question of whether Musk is capable of empathy at all. This is a man who tells his wife that “if you were my employee, I would fire you”, and urges her to tell his estranged trans-daughter Jenna that “I’ll always love her” – and then cuts off her health insurance the next day.

Musk knew with a disconcerting degree of certainty that Trump would re-elected

In the film, St Clair describes the events of Trump’s election in November 2024. Musk, she tells Gibney, had a “degree of certainty” about the results before they came in that “I had never seen before”. He told her that he would “unleash the anomaly in the matrix” and that “we have 10,000 lasers in space”. Gibney leaves that comment hanging.

The godfather of AI is worried Musk might rig the next election

Geoffrey Hinton, the Nobel-winning British-Canadian computer scientist known as the “godfather of AI”, used to be friendly with Musk, but the pair fell out after Hinton declined his offer to join the xAI board. In the film, he makes clear that he does not trust Musk to weigh up the risks and benefits of AI responsibly, and there’s more. “It’s fairly clear to me that Trump is hell-bent on corrupting the midterm elections,” Hinton says onscreen. “If you wanted to corrupt those midterm elections and you wanted to use AI, all you needed to do was get detailed information on US citizens. And what Doge did looked like just what you would do.”

title: Blue Jays Nation Challenges ‘Petulant Child’ Donald Trump After Lake America Update
description: The Toronto Blue Jays were at the center of political debate after U.S. President Donald Trump renamed Lake Ontario amid a trade dispute.
fullText:
The Toronto Blue Jays spent one of their final series of the regular season turning a road stadium into something resembling home games, with fans traveling across the border to support a team fighting for an American League playoff spot.

During Toronto's recent series against the Cleveland Guardians, a matchup that carried major wild-card implications, Blue Jays fans traveled en masse. The Blue Jays won the season series and, in the process, secured an important tiebreaker that could become critical if the teams finish with identical records.

"The Blue Jays hold the tiebreaker over the Guardians after winning the season series earlier this week," Sportsnet noted on Monday. "Both teams have 18 games remaining."

But the Toronto-Cleveland series also carried some political weight as the teams' respective nations engage in a tense trade war with significant rhetorical implications.

Dodgers' Pending $400 Million Free Agent Could 'Gravitate' Toward Angels Contract

The recent Guardians series provided a striking reminder of how many Blue Jays supporters cross the U.S.-Canada border to follow their team.

"If you closed your eyes, you might have thought the Blue Jays were playing at home," Mike Wilner reported for the Toronto Star. "Over a three-game series with huge playoff implications, every Jays' run was met with loud cheers and there were several spontaneous chants of 'Let's go Blue Jays!' that rained down from the seats at Progressive Field in Cleveland, which sits at the corner of Ontario Street and Carnegie Avenue."

That cross-border connection took on a different dimension after President Donald Trump issued an executive order directing the federal government to rename Lake Ontario as "Lake America."

The White House order, signed August 27, directs the Interior Department and Board on Geographic Names to take steps to rename the body of water and update the federal Geographic Names Information System. The order describes the lake as an important American economic and strategic asset.

The decision has drawn attention in Canada, particularly because Lake Ontario is shared by the United States and Canada. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has continued referring to the body of water as Lake Ontario.

And for several Blue Jays fan attending the Cleveland series, the political dispute couldn't be ignored.

Joshua Glass, travelling with a friend who gracefully exited the conversation when he heard what the topic was going to be, doesn't share his fellow fans' hesitance.

"I'm not going to pay attention to the rantings of a petulant child, quite frankly," said Joshua Glass, one Blue Jays fan in attendance in Cleveland, according to Wilner. "It's not going to keep me from going to see my team fight for a wild-card spot. I think the whole thing is a bit ridiculous, but it's not going to prevent me from coming ... I'm going to be here no matter what. Until they close the border, that is."

While the political dispute didn't seem to turn Blue Jays away from supporting their favorite team in Cleveland, several of them indicated that Trump's latest geographic moniker decision did give them second thoughts about visiting the U.S.

"After the whole 'Lake America'/Lake Ontario thing," a fan named Melissa told Wilner. "You kind of get numb to the whole 'We're going to charge you tariffs' and everything like that, but as it just escalates now you just kind of get turned off from wanting to come, but I'm going to love the game."

Member Of Yankees' Legendary World Series Championship Roster Dies

For the Blue Jays, the larger story remains the playoff race. Toronto and Cleveland were separated by the thinnest of margins entering the final stretch, making their season series particularly significant.

And the passionate Cleveland turnout demonstrated that Toronto's fan base remains willing to travel when the stakes rise. With the Blue Jays pursuing a wild-card berth, that support could continue to follow them throughout the postseason chase.

title: Pistol-packing man knocks over fairgoers forcing his way toward Ohio governor candidate Amy Acton, police say
description: Amy Acton's campaign says the Ohio governor candidate was targeted by an armed individual at the Canfield Fair as political violence fears mount.
fullText:
An armed man forced his way through a crowd toward Ohio gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton, knocking over multiple fairgoers before troopers stopped him at the Canfield Fair, authorities said.

Troopers assigned to the Ohio State Highway Patrol's executive protection unit intercepted Patrick M. Havas, 38, during the Sept. 6 incident, according to a statement provided by the Ohio Department of Public Safety to Fox News Digital.

"Havas knocked multiple fairgoers over while trying to get towards Dr. Acton, and was found to be in possession of a taser and two pistols," the highway patrol said. "Dr. Acton was unharmed during the incident."

Havas was turned over first to Canfield Fair Police and then to the Mahoning County Sheriff's Office before being taken to the county jail, according to the statement.

Trump's Decade Of Assassination Threats Runs From Butler Shooting To Latest Golf Club Breach

He was booked on two counts of assault and one count of disorderly conduct. A jail record listed Havas as being held in pretrial custody.

The highway patrol and sheriff's office are investigating what led to the confrontation. No additional details were immediately available.

Acton's campaign initially said an armed individual had lunged at the candidate and injured multiple people.

"While attending the Canfield Fair, an armed individual lunged at Dr. Acton, injuring multiple people," Acton campaign communications director Addie Bullock said in a statement.

"Dr. Acton and Eric are grateful for the swift and decisive action of law enforcement and are praying for the recovery of those injured," Bullock added. "This kind of violence has no place in Ohio. Dr. Acton will always stand up to the chaos, hate and vitriol that pits us against one another."

Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine later confirmed that Acton was not hurt and said he and first lady Fran DeWine spoke with her following the incident.

"Fran and I are thankful Dr. Amy Acton was not hurt, and we send our thoughts to those who were injured," DeWine said. "We spoke to Dr. Acton this afternoon and she said to share with Ohioans that she is ok."

DeWine said a man "tried to forcefully push himself toward Dr. Acton" as she was speaking and injured other attendees at the Mahoning County Democratic booth.

"We are grateful for the quick work of the Ohio State Highway Patrol and other law enforcement on the scene at the Canfield Fair today," the governor said.

"Violence or the threat of violence at political or public events is always unacceptable," DeWine added. "This case is now in the hands of law enforcement and will be investigated thoroughly."

The incident came as Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin warned that candidates and other public figures continue to face threats as campaign season kicks into high gear.

"You're never safe in the public eye," Mullin told Fox News' Peter Doocy during an interview on "The Sunday Briefing."

White House Correspondents' Dinner Shooting Latest In Years Of Attacks Targeting Trump, Conservatives

Doocy asked Mullin whether candidates were safe heading into the traditional Labor Day weekend kickoff to campaign season, citing the political assassinations and assassination attempts that have rocked the country in recent years.

"If you read any of the social media posts, which I choose not to, but you see the type of rhetoric and the hatefulness that's out there," Mullin said.

Dem Senate Hopefuls Under Scrutiny For 'Choke Them Out' Rhetoric After Trump Attack Scare

"The threats to our elected officials, they don't go away," he continued. "We've got to bring down the temperature, but the temperature is not going to go down on itself."

Mullin said Americans must accept that political disagreements are part of the country's system of government while drawing a firm line at violence.

West Virginia Man Pleads Guilty To Making Violent Threats Against Trump, Ice

"The American people have to realize that we do have a republic, and the republic has different opinions, and it's OK to have different opinions," he said.

"When you cross a line and say that that different opinion needs to be silenced — it needs to be silenced through violence — that's where Homeland comes into place," Mullin added. "Free speech is something we all protect, but there's a line that you can cross that goes from free speech to inciting dangerous behavior."

Mullin was speaking broadly about political threats and was not responding directly to the reported confrontation involving Acton.

Republican gubernatorial nominee Vivek Ramaswamy and his running mate, Ohio Senate President Rob McColley, condemned the Canfield Fair incident.

"Candidates should be able to meet with voters without having to worry about threats or violence," Ramaswamy campaign communications director Connie Luck said in a statement.

"What happened today is completely unacceptable and has no place in politics, and we hope that no one was hurt," she added.

Ramaswamy Outlines Key Contrasts With Dem Opponent Less Than 100 Days Out From Key Gubernatorial Election

Acton and Ramaswamy are facing off in November's closely watched race to replace term-limited Republican Gov. Mike DeWine.

Acton, a physician, became a household name in Ohio while serving as director of the Ohio Department of Health during the COVID-19 pandemic, according to The Associated Press. She appeared alongside DeWine during televised briefings as the state imposed shutdowns and other public-health restrictions.

Her handling of the pandemic has since become a central campaign issue, The AP reported. Ramaswamy and other Republicans have criticized Acton over the restrictions, while her campaign has defended her work with DeWine as necessary to protect Ohioans.

Fox News Digital reached out to the Mahoning County Sheriff's Office for additional information.

Fox News' Peter Doocy contributed to this report.

fullText:
Politicians on the right and left are pushing back against Flock as more Americans voice opposition to the tech

Growing factions from both sides of the political aisle in the US are pushing back against surveillance cameras made by a single company, a rare response in a sharply divided country with a president pushing an unwaveringly pro-tech agenda.

The bipartisan backlash against Flock Safety cameras resembles nationwide rage toward the construction of large datacenters that power artificial intelligence. Polling shows roughly 75% of Americans oppose new datacenter construction in their areas.

Flock’s cameras are automated license plate readers (ALPRs), which take pictures of vehicle license plates so police and security companies can log the movement of cars in a given area. There are about 120,000 Flock cameras across the US, which conduct roughly 2bn scans per month. The company is staring down controversy after reports of abuses of its cameras by police officers in multiple states, who have used them to stalk ex-lovers and track people seeking abortions. The network the cameras feed into is also frequently utilized by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

Data and polling from the Washington Post show that social media posts about Flock have increased since July, and about 46% of Americans oppose ALPRs being used in their community – up 13 points from the previous year. Vigilantes are posting videos of themselves destroying the cameras to digital applause. According to privacy and surveillance experts, hatred of Flock cameras has become bipartisan.

“In my 20-plus years at the ACLU, I’ve never really seen such a grassroots uprising against surveillance technology like this,” said Jay Stanley, a senior policy analyst at the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU). “On the left, there’s a historical memory of law enforcement spying on and interfering with advocates for social change … On the right, there’s a long tradition of ‘don’t tread on me’ – keep the government out of my life, keep it from looking over my shoulder.”

Both liberal and conservative politicians are pushing back against Flock cameras. Greg Abbott, Texas’s Republican governor, blocked state agencies from procuring Flock products. On the other side of the political spectrum, Bernie Sanders, the progressive US senator, is promising to introduce legislation to restrict the use of Flock cameras. Republican senator Josh Hawley has launched an investigation into potential Flock privacy abuses, and Democratic congressman Ro Khanna is cosponsoring a bill with Republican congressman Thomas Massie to prevent federal funds from being used to purchase Flock cameras.

Municipal leaders of all political stripes are dropping contracts with Flock, though sometimes they replace the license plate readers with another brand of camera and continue the surveillance. We reached out to Flock Safety for a statement and did not receive a response before publishing.

Surveillance hasn’t always been a unifying topic in US politics. Debates over the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (Fisa), the Patriot Act and other surveillance issues have often been divisive. This appears to be an unusual case where politicians are getting on the same side of a hot-button issue.

“Privacy, to some extent, is bipartisan,” said Matthew Guariglia, a senior policy analyst at the Electronic Frontier Foundation. “When you put up these cameras, they last longer than the current administration. You might trust the people in power now who put them up – but are you going to trust the next people who get access to that equipment?”

Americans have been showing up at town hall meetings by the dozen over the past six months or so, and there have been numerous protests to show opposition to Flock surveillance cameras around the country. More than 100 jurisdictions have canceled their contracts so far, according to data from the non-profit Institute for Justice. An organization called DeFlock, founded in 2024, hopes to increase the numbers by compiling a map of the cameras’ locations.

While ALPRs aren’t new, Flock, founded in 2017, has made them far more prevalent than they used to be. The company’s software allows disparate law enforcement agencies to share data with one another, meaning a license plate scan by a police department in one state could easily and quickly be used in another.

“Flock represents tech companies in bed with governments, doing the exact stuff people have become distrustful of and resentful about for the past few decades. It feels like it’s finally hit the boiling-over point,” said Woodrow Hartzog, a professor of law and computer science at Boston University.

Hartzog predicts the actions against Flock Safety will continue at the state and local level amid this growing popular outrage. He expects people are going to stay angry about the issue, and politicians will have to respond.

“The pushback we’re seeing against Flock cameras is one of the most vivid illustrations I can think of that surveillance is not inevitable – that these tools aren’t inevitable,” Hartzog says. “It’s up to all of us to stop them.”

title: Supreme Court grants Republican emergency appeal on TV ad rates before midterms
description: The Supreme Court granted an emergency appeal from Republicans in a dispute over campaign ad prices on Friday, clearing a legal roadblock to political parties getting cheaper TV ad time ahead of the m...
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Supreme Court granted an emergency appeal from Republicans in a dispute over campaign ad prices on Friday, clearing a legal roadblock to political parties getting cheaper TV ad time ahead of the midterm elections.

The justices halted for now a lower-court ruling in favor of Democratic candidates who argued that cheaper broadcast ads should be limited to candidates. One justice publicly dissented from the unsigned order. It's the latest election-related appeal to come before the high court ahead of the pivotal November contests.

The Trump administration supported the emergency appeal from GOP campaign arms.

The decision comes on the heels of a June Supreme Court ruling that removed limits on parties spending money in coordination with candidates. It was seen as a boon to the GOP because the national party has a sizable cash advantage, and access to cheaper ad rates could boost that edge.

Among Democrats, meanwhile, some individual candidates have sizable fundraising advantages over their Republican opponents.

Candidates pay discounted rates for TV time around an election under federal law, and in March the Federal Communications Commission's Media Bureau said certain party-coordinated ads are entitled to those prices as well.

Four Democrats, including Sen. Jon Ossoff of Georgia and former Sen. Sherrod Brown of Ohio, challenged the finding in court. They won a victory from a divided panel of the U.S. 4th Circuit Court of appeals.

The National Republican Congressional Committee and National Republican Senatorial Committee then asked the Supreme Court to intervene. They argued that broadcasters were already charging them higher rates and upending their planned budgets after the appeals court decision.

The majority of justices agreed that the lower court had acted too soon with the order that differed from judges around the country.

"Current and future recissions will require the party committees to pay more for advertising space, thereby hampering their efforts to reach the electorate in the critical weeks leading up to the midterms," the Supreme Court order states.

One justice, Ketanji Brown Jackson, disagreed, writing that the court likely didn't have to wait until an internal FCC review was done.

The decision halts the appeals court ruling while the Republican committees file a fuller appeal.

EXCLUSIVE — The head of an influential Senate committee is urging Congress to reconsider the charter of the nation's largest teachers union, citing its far-left associations and allegedly irresponsible financial activity.

In recent years, the National Education Association, which represents roughly 3 million educators, has come under fire for mobilizing students and teachers to support liberal activist campaigns, been criticized by its Jewish members for failing to address antisemitism, spent millions in membership dues supporting left-wing causes and partnered with organizations that portray political violence and far-left extremism favorably.

Now, Sen. Bill Cassidy, the Republican chair of the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions, is calling on his colleagues to take a closer look at the NEA's congressional charter.

Blistering Report Exposes How National K-12 Group's Dei Agenda Is Trickling Down To Local Schools

"Children are struggling to read and to do basic math. Instead of helping students succeed, teachers' unions are injecting a dangerous, anti-American agenda into our classrooms," Cassidy told Fox News Digital. "Parents deserve to send their children to school without worrying that they will be indoctrinated with Dei and taught that Americans have 'misplaced faith' in our institutions."

Cassidy, in a report outlining the NEA's activity obtained exclusively by Fox News Digital, puts a spotlight on the Zinn Education Project and Rethinking Schools — a pair of interlinked educational nonprofits that the top teachers union has collaborated with extensively.

Exclusive: Splc's 'Far-left' 'Anti-racism' Curriculum Found In Classrooms As Early As Kindergarten: Watchdog

The Zinn Education Project and Rethinking Schools, for instance, have published curricular materials that justify the actions of the Black Panther Party — a left-wing militant Black nationalist organization that operated during the Cold War — and praise its members, including those who were involved in acts of political violence, according to the report.

"The Marxist and communist ideologies espoused by the Black Panther Party are inconsistent and incompatible with the foundation of the United States Constitution," Cassidy's report, published by the HELP committee, reads. "The Black Panthers advocated for the use of armed force against police and were involved in the murders of civil servants and members of their own party."

Scope Of Splc's Deeply Embedded Influence Training Teachers Nationwide Uncovered In Sweeping Report

Rethinking Schools also published a lesson plan where students are meant to role-play as "queer liberation" activists fighting against the "Religious Right," according to the report. Another lesson plan, titled "Expanding Intersectional Queer History in the Elementary Grades," instructs teachers on how to incorporate LGBTQ material into lessons for young students.

The union has worked closely with the duo of nonprofits over the years, giving them prominent space and speaking opportunities at conferences, collaborating with them on curriculum development and nationwide teaching events, and praising and promoting their lessons. The union has also incorporated the groups' work into educator handbooks and helped distribute their lesson plans to teachers.

House Gop Launches Probe Into 5 Major Labor Unions Over Dem Spending Despite Maga Membership Base

Congress chartered the NEA in 1906 under the expectation that it would "elevate the character and advance the interests of the profession of teaching; and to promote the cause of education in the United States," a mission Cassidy and some other Republicans argue it has since strayed from. Revoking the NEA's charter would primarily be a reputational blow to the union, as it would still be able to operate even without it.

As another example of the NEA allegedly failing to live up to its charter, the HELP committee points to its involvement in the left-wing protest movements.

May Day Protests 'Just The Beginning' Of Student Activism Push, Expert Warns

The labor union promoted and participated in the 2026 May Day protests, which were critical of President Donald Trump and his Republican allies. In one planning webinar the NEA hosted in the lead-up to the demonstrations, educators were advised to "bring activism into the classroom," targeting children as young as three years old. Students in Chicago were reportedly encouraged by teachers to skip class for the protests, even as Chicago Public Schools see subpar reading and math competency scores.

On the financial side of things, Cassidy points to data showing that, since 2015, the NEA has contributed hundreds of millions of dollars to advocacy organizations and political action committees, the vast majority of which are left-of-center. In some cases, political organizations funded by the NEA later provided members of the union's leadership team with cushy jobs, according to the report.

Far-left Activist Conference At Teachers Union Hq Raises Classroom Concerns

"The central issue is not whether every such expenditure is impermissible. Rather, it is whether members receive sufficient transparency about how their dues are used, whether union leadership has adopted adequate safeguards against conflicts of interest and whether these expenditures advance the purposes for which members joined the union in the first place," the Senate committee report reads.

Organizations funded by the NEA include the Sixteen Thirty Fund and the Tides Foundation, two of the largest Democratic-aligned dark money operations in the country, as well as millions to its own PAC, which almost exclusively supports Democratic candidates.

Jewish Educators Face Rampant Antisemitism In Teachers Unions, New Report Finds

The HELP committee report also alleges that the NEA has failed to represent the interests of Jewish educators, citing an August 2025 letter where the union's Jewish Affairs Caucus claimed its members reported "shunning, harassment and antisemitic comments" at the union's annual assembly.

While not congressionally chartered like the NEA, the American Federation of Teachers drew flak from Cassidy's report for many of the same reasons.

The report cites the AFT's participation in "No Kings" protests against President Donald Trump, its boycott of Target over immigration enforcement and its advocacy on LGBTQ+ issues, as well as its routing of tens of millions of dollars to liberal causes, as evidence of alleged mission drift at the union.

The NEA, AFT, Rethinking Schools and the Zinn Education Project did not respond to requests for comment when reached by Fox News Digital on Tuesday.

The scrutiny comes as the NEA transitions to new leadership. Princess R. Moss, a former NEA vice president and secretary-treasurer, began a three-year term as president on Tuesday, succeeding Becky Pringle, who led the union for six years.

Former President Joe Biden's son, Hunter Biden, said Sunday that former Vice President Kamala Harris was getting bad political advice after he refused to explain why he thinks she wasn't a good politician.

Zeteo founder and former MSNBC host Mehdi Hasan pressed Biden on why he said that Harris was "not a very good politician" despite her repeatedly refusing to break from Joe Biden on key issues while campaigning in 2024.

"Here's what I'd also like to say about the vice president. I think that the vice president served the country incredibly well and that she has a deep, rich future in politics. Whether she wants to run for president again, she'll be one of the, if not, the frontrunner," he said.

Hasan pressed, "But she's not a very good politician?"

Hunter Biden Reveals He Never Wanted Joe Biden To Run For Re-election, But Refused To Tell Him To Stop

"No, and I think that the way that she's going about it right now is, at least from my perspective …," Biden began, as Hasan pressed him to elaborate.

Biden said, "I think that this administration, unlike you, I don't think that she should have ever been any daylight between, she can make daylight between herself and my dad, but not in terms of what they were able to accomplish over that four-year period. I think that there might be daylight as issues related to Gaza and as it relates to Israel that of course, she needs to be able to stake her own ground on that."

The Zeteo founder noted that Harris didn't really break from Biden on Gaza or Israel.

Biden insisted Harris' refusal to break with his father on the issue didn't have anything to do with his father.

"He didn't pressure her? No daylight, kid?" Hasan asked.

A post-2024 election book by reporters Jonathan Allen and Amie Parnes said Joe Biden had told Harris repeatedly that there could be "no daylight" between them and reported that he told her, "No daylight, kid," during a call ahead of her debate with Donald Trump.

Kamala Harris Leaves Biden Off List Of Top Three 'Most Effective' Presidents

The former president denied doing this during an interview on "The View."

"Nothing to do with loyalty to my dad, from my perspective. But here's the thing, is this, is that, you know what? She's a free agent now. I'm Hunter Biden," he said. "I get to think whatever the hell that I want to think about anybody."

Hasan pressed him again, questioning, "I'm asking why do you think she's not a very good politician?"

"That's between me and her," Hunter Biden told Hasan.

Hasan responded and said, "You can't just dangle that out."

Hunter Biden Reveals He's 'Definitely Not Running' For Office Despite Media Tour

"You know why I can? Because I ain't running for anything, Mehdi, I can say whatever the f--- I want," Biden shot back.

Hunter Biden said he did not agree with the perspective that Harris was loyal to his father throughout her campaign.

"I think that she was loyal to my father, and I don't think she was loyal to a fault, however. There are certain things she was not loyal on. Later in the interview, during a discussion about a possible 2028 ticket, Biden said he would love for Harris to be president of the United States.

"I would love for her to be president of the United States. I think she would make a great president of the United States. I just think that, right now, she's getting bad political advice. That's it," he said.

title: ‘Scary’: how misinformation and AI hallucinations are infiltrating Australia’s parliament
description: Exclusive: Guardian analysis reveals that dozens of policy submissions from across the political spectrum incorrectly summarise real research and invent or wrongly cite...
fullText:
Exclusive: Guardian analysis reveals that dozens of policy submissions from across the political spectrum incorrectly summarise real research and invent or wrongly cite sources

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Australia’s government inquiry process is supposed to help parliament make better decisions, hearing from experts and constituents alike. But Guardian Australia can reveal that the system is being flooded with AI-generated material, which is inventing studies and attributing nonexistent research to real academics and authors.

In some cases, committee reports have cited submissions in which the majority of sources appear to be AI-generated “hallucinations”, when large language models (LLMs) invent content that looks real but doesn’t actually exist.

An AI hallucination takes place when an LLM like ChatGPT or Claude outputs text that is plausible but incorrect, or confidently generates information that appears relevant but is actually unrelated.

This happens because these AI systems use complex statistics to figure out the text they generate and they have no innate ability to distinguish between correct and incorrect content. They simply predict the next most likely bit of text based on their training data, with a certain degree of creativity or randomness involved.

Hallucinations can become more common when the AI is asked to generate content on topics that are not well covered in its training data.

These hallucinations are not bugs and although the frequency can be reduced by increasing the amount of training data or adding web-search results and other information, they are an inherent feature of LLMs and can never be fully eliminated.

If the phenomenon continues, there is a significant risk of parliamentarians “making decisions based on evidence that doesn’t exist”, says Christian Downie, a professor in the Australian National University’s school of regulation and global governance.

The situation is made more confusing by AI services including Google search. Previously, looking up an invented reference might produce results that would indicate the reference did not exist. Now Google’s AI summary will sometimes create summaries of a fake reference as though it were genuine.

In some instances, Google’s AI summary and ChatGPT will also cite the inquiry submission with the fake reference as a source, creating an ongoing cycle of misinformation.

One document submitted to an inquiry into family violence and suicide included a hallucinated reference attributed to Divna Haslam, a University of Queensland associate professor and clinical psychologist, and misstated her team’s research findings.

Haslam, who researches child and family adversity and maltreatment, says the reference was “scary” because it looked so real that someone taking a cursory look could be convinced. Google’s AI summary summarised the reference as if it were a real paper.

“It’s very frustrating to … to have invested time, money, effort, expertise in rigorous research,” she says. “Then to see something that’s inaccurate and inappropriately attributed anyway is really concerning.”

The author of the submission, Drilldown Reports, told Guardian Australia it used AI in its research process and had identified the errors in its follow-up submission – but the deadline had passed to have them corrected.

“We do strongly believe in the human factor and that it should be a vital part of the full quality review process,” a spokesperson said. “Unfortunately, the human factor also lets us down when uploading the correct document.

“I get that you feel you have a juicy article to add the AI fear machine but this was a human error, not AI.”

The chair of the standing committee on social policy and legal affairs, which oversaw the inquiry, said all committees received a range of materials of varying quality and positions: “It is the job of the committee to both accept the evidence offered on face value but then also interrogate it through the inquiry process.”

Haslam says not only does this phenomenon risk devaluing legitimate research but there are serious risks if misleading information makes its way into government policy. “Particularly in a [domestic violence] space,” she says. “We just can’t risk that.”

The paper was just one of dozens the Guardian identified by building a computer program that extracted references from all inquiry submissions made to the current parliament and checked those references against several online academic databases.

Documents that were flagged as having a high proportion of references not matching anything were then manually checked.

All current commercial services for AI detection have one important limitation – they get it wrong sometimes. A “false positive” detection can lead people to be falsely accused of using AI services such as ChatGPT or Claude.

For this reason, we took a different approach. Analysis of reports produced with AI and studies on AI-generated journal articles showed that LLMs can often produce references that are incorrect in some way, from getting pages, titles and authors wrong to making up details entirely.

We built a custom program that extracts references from documents and then searches those references in CrossRef (a database of academic papers and books) and Google Scholar. We also programmatically checked digital object identifiers (DOIs) if they were present, to see if they resolved to a reachable URL.

Documents that had 20% or more references that were unable to be matched were then checked manually and a large number of submissions with incorrect references were checked with the original authors to verify our method.

It's important to note that this method can only be used to point towards AI usage in documents with references and so will always be an underestimate of actual AI usage.

All links within documents were also checked for ChatGPT metadata tags. These are tags added by ChatGPT when it provides links to users and can persist when copied into a document. ChatGPT tags do not necessarily indicate that someone used ChatGPT directly, as they could be copying the text from a third-party article or similar.

Using these methods, the Guardian found at least 39 submissions to political inquiries containing what appear to be hallucinated references.

These findings represent a conservative estimate of the amount of AI-generated material in political processes, as it only identifies submissions with incorrect citations. This approach would not find documents that used AI to generate text without any references, for example.

In another indication of how often LLMs are being used, more than 100 papers included ChatGPT url tags in reference links, which are automatically added by the platform in its results.

The submissions containing AI-generated material range from documents with a small number of incorrect citations to submissions in which every reference cited does not exist. They were authored by individuals and organisations across the political spectrum.

When Guardian Australia contacted the people and organisations responsible, many were unaware AI could get things wrong in this way or were aware of the potential for errors but had missed them before submitting the document.

How governments will grapple with AI-generated errors in material intended to influence policy, or whether they have the tools and resources to identify them, is an emerging question. Last year the consultancy giant Deloitte issued a partial refund to the federal government after it was revealed that AI tools had included fake references and even a fake court reference in a $440,000 report.

Downie says if public documents like government submissions or even court judgments are found to contain fake material or fake citations, the implications could go beyond bad decisions.

“We’re also starting to undermine the public’s trust and confidence in the types of institutions that underpin our democracy,” he says.

While misleading claims or invented citations are not a new problem, greater access to LLMs has allowed this to grow at unprecedented levels.

One submission to a housing inequity inquiry this year included what appears to be references to work by Nicole Gurran, an academic at the University of Sydney, that does not exist.

Transparency and contestability are a vital part of the research and peer-review process, which is why citations are used as evidence to back up claims, says Gurran, a professor of urban and regional planning.

“Fake citations, even if an accidental ‘collage’ where the claim is correct but the chain of reference to evidence is broken, undermines that,” she says.

Another paper submitted last year to a Senate inquiry into climate change misinformation by the National Rational Energy Network said the Guardian was “left-leaning, activist-oriented” – and appeared to attribute that claim in part to an “article” by Margaret Simons, a journalist and academic, in a top journal.

But Simons – who is on the board of the Guardian’s owner, the Scott Trust – never wrote such a paper.

The endnote so accurately replicated other references that Simons briefly wondered whether it really existed. “Even though I know I didn’t write this, I did have that moment of self-questioning,” she says.

NREN did not respond to a request for comment.

Senate advice for inquiry submissions warns that use of AI can present risks to the quality of information and that accuracy is the responsibility of the submitter.

Downie says the inquiry process needs to remain as open as possible but new guidelines may be needed to “encourage truthfulness”.

“Whether it’s climate change, immigration, health, we want our elected officials to be making decisions based on real information and real evidence not on fake citations and fake claims,” he says.

Guardian Australia asked OpenAI and Google how the companies were working to combat their role in the spread of misinformation.

OpenAI said addressing hallucinations was an ongoing area of research and that users should “use ChatGPT as a first draft, not a final source”, ensuring that they verified quotes, data or references to external documents.

A Google spokesperson said AI Overviews operated “like traditional Search” in that they aimed to match content from the web to the words in the query: “AI Overviews – like traditional blue link results – will find and surface the web pages that include those terms.”

fullText:
Bryce Gustafson has been knocking on doors in Indiana for more than a decade. The lead organizer with Citizens Action Coalition (CAC), a consumer and environmental organization, he usually encounters a mix of reactions when he’s out canvassing; whatever issue he’s talking about, there’s always at least a few people on the other side. But at a recent festival in the rural town of Monrovia, Indiana, he was struck by an unusual spirit of unity.

He was there about a proposed datacenter, a 550-acre (222-hectare) Google project in this small town of 1,600 people. “I had 50 people I talked to,” Gustafson told me. “Nobody wanted that datacenter in their community. And at least a half a dozen people came up to me to say, ‘Hey, I voted for Trump. What the heck’s he doing, supporting these things?’”

Gustafson said he’s had similar conversations all across the state. If there’s one thing he sees uniting Hoosiers of all stripes – from rural areas such as Morgan county to suburbs such as Franklin Township to the historically African American neighborhood of Martindale-Brightwood in Indianapolis – it’s fury over these water-guzzling, air-polluting behemoths and the tech oligarchs imposing them.

These dynamics are playing out across the US. Over the last year, intensifying waves of local opposition to big tech’s datacenter buildout have surged into a nationwide tsunami of resistance. Elites on both coasts, from leaders of the AI industry in Silicon Valley to leaders of the political establishment in Washington DC, have struggled to make sense of the backlash. First they tried to write it off as business-as-usual nimbyism: just a few local bans passed here and there, maybe some unknown city councilors losing re-election after signing datacenter deals – not such a big deal. Then senator Bernie Sanders and congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez began calling for a national moratorium. Pretty soon Utah’s senate president got tossed out of office for supporting hyperscale proposals. And the movement continues to grow.

Today, three-quarters of Americans oppose local datacenter development, a swing of more than 30 points in just a year. More than 500 counties and municipalities have passed datacenter bans or moratoria, while dozens of proposed projects have been killed outright. And the issue has come to define some of the highest-profile political races in the country. In the battle for US Senate in Ohio, populist Democrat Sherrod Brown has made Republican senator Jon Husted’s support of datacenters the centerpiece of his campaign, prompting warnings from the National Republican senatorial committee that “datacenters are the anchor hanging around Husted’s neck”.

Other Republicans are taking notice. The Texas governor, Greg Abbott once touted the state as the “epicenter of AI development”; last week he said datacenters had “dug their own grave”. In Michigan, days after The Lever news outlet revealed that GOP Senate candidate Mike Rogers held millions in AI-related investments, he announced his support for a one-year moratorium on their construction in the state.

Big tech billionaires may finally be beginning to realize that this backlash poses real complications for them. But they still don’t understand the nature of the threat they’ve called down upon themselves, because the movement against datacenters represents more than just a series of local fights against a new kind of infrastructure project. It may, in fact, constitute the best opportunity we’ve had in generations to truly shake up American politics, by redirecting the partisan anger that oligarchic forces have long used to divide regular Americans and channeling that energy instead against the billionaires that are actually the cause of so many of our shared problems.

The political science term for this strategy, coined by Jennifer McCoy and Murat Somer, is “transformative repolarization”. McCoy and Somer argue that authoritarians and oligarchs often stoke what they call “pernicious polarization” – extreme toxic polarization that uses “us versus them” rhetoric, often on social and culture war issues, to divide the public in ways that harm democracy. In the face of such intense suspicion and distrust, depolarizing a society – trying to get people to stop viewing their fellow citizens as an existential danger – may not work on its own, in the absence of a unifying struggle to address underlying grievances. Instead, McCoy and Somer argue that opponents of authoritarianism need to redraw the lines of contestation that define their politics – to shift the “us versus them” struggle from, for example, a left-to-right polarization, to a different axis of conflict that can bring a large majority of the public together against real structural threats.

When you speak to organizers and community leaders on the frontlines of local datacenter campaigns, it immediately becomes clear that they are seeing new configurations of people coming together in precisely this way. “On many issues, people come in with a baked-in partisan lens that influences their thinking,” said Ben Inskeep, program director at CAC. “On datacenters, we don’t have those firm camps formed. And so we’re seeing broad concern from Republicans, Democrats and everyone else on the political spectrum. We’re seeing folks saying, ‘Hey, I might be a Maga Republican and you might be a liberal yahoo from the big city, but if you’re coming to our community to help us fight this datacenter, you’re my best friend.’”

William Lawrence has been seeing the same thing in Michigan. The Sunrise Movement co-founder and congressional candidate made opposition to datacenters a main focus of his successful campaign for the Democratic nomination to represent the Lansing area. He’s now hammering his Republican opponent on the issue – to great apparent effect, according to a recent poll finding Lawrence leading in the district, which is now held by a Republican. “At a time when people are so polarized and isolated from each other, something that brings people together is rare,” he said. “We can all get together to watch the Spartans play at Spartan Stadium, but to get together in a context where you’re also talking about politics? That is a gift, and is not at all to be taken for granted.”

An organizer I spoke with who’s been opposing datacenter construction in Texas (who asked to remain anonymous) noted a similar dynamic playing out in his state. “I’ve never seen anything that mobilizes this many rural Texans before,” he told me. “Folks are starting to get politicized through this work. They’re realizing when they reach out to their state reps, their state senators, that these people are not batting for them. They’re batting for the tech oligarchs. And so people are realizing that the left-to-right divide isn’t as important as the divide between the working class and big corporate interests.”

The electoral implications of this process should be obvious. But for anyone too thick to draw their own conclusions, voters themselves are starting to get quite explicit. When MS Now asked a woman in Hood county, Texas, which is 80% Republican, “you’re willing to forgo every conservative issue and let the Senate fall into the hands of Democrats if that’s what it takes to kill datacenters?”, her response was immediate: “Yep. My entire community’s going to break rank.”

What remains to be seen is whether Democrats will seize this opportunity – or let Republicans regain the initiative.

“I’ve been waiting a long time for people to wake up to how they’re being ripped off,” Gustafson said. So why are datacenters the issue that’s finally waking people up?

For one, they’re essentially unique in the breadth of their odiousness, so everyone has a reason to be offended by them. Hyperscale datacenters are big industrial warehouses that can cover literally dozens of acres, generate debilitating noise pollution, and severely impact local water tables. They use obscene amounts of energy, straining local infrastructure and in many cases causing utility rates to spike. This also has devastating climate and environmental impacts, as AI developers are overwhelmingly meeting their energy needs with dirty fossil fuel generators that spew outrageous amounts of planet-warming emissions and severely impact local air quality.

Then there are the process concerns: use of eminent domain, the provision of taxpayer subsidies, and big tech’s near-ubiquitous practice of pushing local officials to sign nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) that shroud deals in suspicious opacity.

And all of this is for what? Though the development of datacenters creates temporary construction work, once developed, the facilities do not provide communities with significant long-term jobs. The only thing these sites produce (other than many shades of pollution) is added compute for a technology that we’ve all been told will soon put billions of people out of work. In the meantime, as we wait to see whether that dystopian future materializes or it was all an economy-wrecking bubble, AI is largely being experienced as the thing making the internet more annoying, our jobs more stressful, surveillance more terrifying, and big tech billionaires – already widely despised – more powerful than ever. It’s not hard to understand why this doesn’t constitute a very compelling case for datacenters.

What it does provide is a perfect canvas on which to illustrate the broader problems with our political and economic system: how a few individuals have all the money and power to control the decisions that impact our lives. “Datacenters are the physical manifestation of the greed and the hubris and the power of the AI oligarchs,” Gustafson said. “That gets people thinking about why we are allowing these tech billionaires to just run roughshod over our state.”

What emerges from this process is a budding sense of solidarity that can extend far beyond the localized concerns that might have brought someone into a particular fight. Gustafson described how organizers from Evansville, a city in south-west Indiana, began supporting groups across the border in Kentucky when fights started ratcheting up there. Elsewhere, a farmer who became the leader of a datacenter fight in Henry county, Indiana, attended a meeting about a proposed project in a neighboring town. “Next thing you know, she’s helping that community, showing up for them, because it’s so much easier getting through this when you have somebody who’s been there and understands,” he said.

As Inskeep put it: “When one campaign ends, people are saying, ‘Hey, we fought ours, now that it’s done, we’re going to go to the next county and help them.’” And that starts a snowball effect. “People are seeing that they’re stronger together. It’s a beautiful thing.”

Clearly, these fights have created an opening for the left. But the politics around datacenters are still very much up for grabs. Democrats should have a strong inherent edge, given that – on this issue, like so many others – Donald Trump has forcefully aligned himself with his buddies in the billionaire class. The president’s aggressive plans to accelerate big tech’s datacenter buildout include opening up federal lands for hyperscaler construction, axing public participation processes in permitting, and even waiving Clean Air Act and Clean Water Act requirements on the radically absurd grounds that datacenter approvals need to be expedited for national security reasons.

But other conservative forces have been ahead of the curve. Steve Bannon has long been working to put Maga’s populist wing out front in opposing both datacenters and AI more broadly. The Texas organizer I spoke with told me he sees a significant number of people coming into datacenter fights casting blame not on big tech oligarchs, but on China or the United Arab Emirates, in ways that can feel decidedly xenophobic or Islamophobic. “This is an opportunity, but it’s a short-lived opportunity and we need to seize it,” said Inskeep. “Because this can also be used against us. If we are not effective at doing the political education and helping folks through that process, I do think you could have a far-right, nationalist, anti-immigrant person use this issue to come to power and then implement horrifying policies.”

Needless to say, for Democrats to seize this opportunity, they first must actually take a unified stance against datacenters. And unfortunately, many Democratic leaders remain just as in-bed with big tech billionaires as their GOP counterparts. Maine’s Democratic governor, Janet Mills vetoed the datacenter moratorium passed by her state legislature. Michigan’s Democratic governor, Gretchen Whitmer was accused of dismissing her constituents’ concerns about the many datacenter projects she has supported. The Democratic minority leader, Hakeem Jeffries opposes a datacenter moratorium and appointed the aggressively corporatist Josh Gottheimer and big tech-backed Zoe Lofgren to help develop House Democrats’ AI platform.

And there are some races where Democrats are squarely on the losing side of the issue. In Wisconsin, the Democratic nominee for governor, David Crowley, is already being blasted in ads by his Republican opponent for having said he wants Wisconsin to “become an AI and a data hub not only for the entire country, but for the entire globe”. Crowley won his gubernatorial primary after the entire Democratic establishment united to oppose the left-leaning candidate in the race, Francesca Hong, on the grounds that old “woke” posts – including a call to “cancel Thanksgiving” – made her unelectable. But Crowley’s troubles demonstrate why Democrats need to update their assumptions regarding what kinds of past statements make for real electoral liabilities. After all, nobody is actually going to cancel Thanksgiving. But making Wisconsin into a hub of hated datacenters? That feels like a very real possibility to a lot of Wisconsin’s swing voters.

When I asked Lawrence what he would want to say to party leadership on this point, his response was simple. “I would say, listen to the people. Nobody wants companies from Silicon Valley coming in, bullying us, making decisions that are going to impact the next century of our communities. Just listen to the people. You’ll be popular.”

So will Democrats take the chance they’ve been given? For the first time in generations, the billionaire class has overreached in a way that Americans of all stripes and ideologies are finding equally repulsive. They’ve created a perfect opening to repolarize the public – not just against Trump, but against the oligarchic and authoritarian systems that produced him in the first place.

The opportunity before us is singular. What a monstrous mistake it would be not to seize it.

Aaron Regunberg is a former Rhode Island state representative and a contributing editor at the New Republic. He is the director of Public Citizen’s Climate Accountability Project, but is writing here in his personal capacity

title: Hong Kong's independent bookstores, a refuge for Chinese readers, are under threat
description: Chinese university student Fleming Cheng found the political books he had only glimpsed online in a Hong Kong bookstore last year.  Before visiting Greenfield Book Store, Cheng had only managed to see...
fullText:
HONG KONG (AP) — Chinese university student Fleming Cheng found the political books he had only glimpsed online in a Hong Kong bookstore last year.

Before visiting Greenfield Book Store, Cheng had only managed to see the books' covers online after bypassing Beijing's internet censorship using a VPN. At the store, he picked up a title offering a critical account of China. He stood there devouring dozens of pages from another, about a pro-reform Chinese leader who fell from power for sympathizing with the protesters during the Tiananmen Square pro-democracy movement in 1989.

Cheng said he saw perspectives diverging from the mainland's official narrative.

Hong Kong's independent bookstores, many of them tucked away from busy streets inside buildings, have long offered a refuge and a window to a freer world for some mainland Chinese readers seeking ideas suppressed at home.

But these spaces now are under threat following a wave of bookseller arrests over alleged sedition under a 2024 national security law. Critics say their plight reflected the city's broader crackdown on dissent that began after Beijing imposed a separate 2020 security law. Authorities say the two laws are vital to stability.

Greenfield was one of four bookstores targeted by police in just four months. Although bail was granted, the 50-year-old shop in July announced it would close at the end of its lease. Another bookstore, Have A Nice Stay, set up by former journalists, had announced plans to shut down Sunday, citing "elusive red lines" and financial challenges, even before its booksellers were arrested on the same day as Greenfield's.

"If the Hong Kong government desperately tries to bring every aspect of the city into close alignment with the mainland, or even to the point where the two become indistinguishable, that would be a tremendous loss for us mainlanders too," Cheng said.

Hong Kong, a former British colony that returned to China in 1997, was once known for its freedoms of publication and expression.

But in 2015, bookseller Lam Wing-kee and four others affiliated with Causeway Bay Books disappeared. The store was known for selling politically sensitive titles. Lam later told reporters he was held by Chinese authorities, providing explosive details that contradicted official Chinese accounts. Gossipy books about Chinese politics soon dwindled on Hong Kong's shelves.

After the 2020 security law, leading activists were arrested and civil society groups disbanded. Titles about the Tiananmen crackdown and works by pro-democracy politicians were pulled from public libraries. At the city's annual book fair, some smaller book businesses were barred from exhibiting, and a pro-Beijing newspaper labeled an independent book fair a form of "soft resistance."

Despite the pressure and increased official inspections, many pressed on, with some continuing to organize activities alongside selling books.

But the arrests hit Book Punch in March, Hunter Bookstore in June, and Greenfield and Have A Nice Stay in July. The authorities accused the booksellers of selling seditious publications, according to government statements and media reports.

Authorities say statements with "seditious intention" to incite hatred against or the overthrow of the governments of China and Hong Kong are prohibited. But they have not specified the books they consider as "seditious," leaving observers to find clues in news reports quoting anonymous sources.

Secretary for Security Chris Tang said the law is clear about what constitutes seditious intent and reiterated there would be no banned book list. He said booksellers should ensure the titles they sell do not harm national security, just as those selling food need to ensure the food won't cause a stomach ache or be poisonous.

A bookseller, who spoke on condition of anonymity for fear of government retribution, said they struggled to judge what was seditious. Still, they became more cautious about whether to sell certain books on China's modern politics. Their landlord was also reviewing whether to continue to rent the space to them after being harassed.

In an emailed reply, the government condemned any "smearing" and false remarks regarding the work in safeguarding national security. It said the security laws clearly stipulate that human rights, freedoms of speech and publication should be protected.

The offenses linked to seditious intention expressly protect expression of opinions or even criticism against government policies, it said.

University student Iris Wang from neighboring Guangdong sensed tighter control over Hong Kong. To her, Hunter encouraged people to think, instead of just selling books like its mainland peers. She bought a postcard about being courageous and a manga there.

Some mainland readers also visit the stores for non-political reasons, such as for their niche books or simply for their calmness.

Hong Konger Brian Leung found companionship in independent bookstores, saying each had its own character. When arrests happened at the shops he visited, he said he felt something he cherished and that Hong Kong deserved was being rejected.

"Part of what I have grown used to in Hong Kong is lost again," he said, adding that the bookshops have not "incited" him because readers can judge for themselves.

In Taiwan, widely seen as the freest publishing hub for Chinese-language books, some publishers have filled the gap as restrictions deepened in Hong Kong after the 2020 security law took effect. Some readers fear one day Taiwan cannot send books to Hong Kong as freely as before.

Taiwan's publishers released six times as many books about Hong Kong between 2020 and 2024 as in the previous five years, according to Cheng Tsu-Bang, a sociology professor at Tunghai University in Taiwan.

"The publication of books seems to have become a very important medium of communication between Taiwan and Hong Kong, or a medium of mutual support," he said.

In July, Taiwan's broadcaster FTV reported that a logistics firm stopped taking orders to ship books from Taiwan to Hong Kong bookstores under investigation. It also demanded a full book list before delivering to other Hong Kong premises, the report added.

One Hong Kong author who moved to Taiwan and has published books there is Lee, who spoke on condition of not using their full name out of fear of government retribution.

Lee has written about Hong Kong's pro-democracy movement, saying the independent bookstores served as a bridge to bring works about Hong Kong to the city and connect diaspora writers to their home.

The writer compared the collapse of civil society to a boulder rolling downhill, crushing things in its path. Lee said bookstores were a small flower field where people could breathe and try to safeguard what remained.

"It's now like being told very directly and cruelly that perhaps this borrowed time is coming to an end," Lee said.

title: Milo Yiannopoulos, a far-right political commentator, detained by ICE
description: A former editor of Breitbart News, Yiannopoulos has also served as an intern for Marjorie Taylor Greene
fullText:
A former editor of Breitbart News, Yiannopoulos has also served as an intern for Marjorie Taylor Greene

Milo Yiannopoulos, a far-right British political commentator, was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Louisiana, according to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).

In a statement on Friday, a DHS spokesperson said that Yiannopoulos was arrested on Thursday at the Louis Armstrong New Orleans international airport (MSY). The spokesperson said Yiannopoulos “legally entered the country” in May 2019, but that “he chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws”.

The spokesperson said Yiannopoulos was issued a final order of removal by an immigration judge on 22 July, “after failing to show up for his immigration hearing”.

“He will remain in ICE custody pending removal,” the spokesperson added. “This administration is working diligently to ensure that aliens in our country illegally can no longer fly unless it is out of our country to self-deport.”

As of Friday afternoon, Yiannopoulos is listed in ICE’s online detainee database as being in “ICE Custody”. The database states that he was born in the United Kingdom, but it does not disclose any additional details, including where he is being held.

The statement comes as multiple outlets reported on Friday that Yiannopoulos had been detained in Louisiana. Fox News reported that Yiannopoulos is currently detained in Alexandria, Lousiana.

Yiannopoulos, a former editor of Breitbart News, previously served as an intern for Marjorie Taylor Greene, a former US representative, in 2022, and also worked on the 2024 White House campaign of Ye, formerly known as Kanye West. It is unclear why Yiannopoulos might have been in Louisiana, but Ye is scheduled to perform in New Orleans on Friday night.

Last year, in posts on social media, Yiannopoulos had been supportive of immigration enforcement in the US.

“California needs ICE checkpoints at supermarket entrances, gas stations, strip malls, intersections and government buildings, with on the spot deportation for anyone who can’t prove they are in the US legally,” he wrote in a social media post in June 2025.

On social media on Friday, Laura Loomer, the far-right activist and ally of Donald Trump, claimed credit for Yiannopoulos’s detention and wrote that she had previously reported him to ICE.

title: New Texas poll shows tight Senate race, GOP pulling ahead for governor
description: Talarico leads Paxton 42-39 in the new UT/Texas Politics Project poll. Abbott leads Hinojosa in the governor's race, and data center opposition holds.
fullText:
Just over two months out from Election Day, a new Texas poll found three notable results: the candidates remain statistically tied in the U.S. Senate race, Republicans are pulling ahead in the governor's race, and Texans are united in their disdain for data centers.

A new University of Texas/Texas Politics Project poll, published Aug. 25, finds 42% of Texas voters preferring Democrat state Rep. James Talarico and 39% planning to vote for Republican state Attorney General Ken Paxton in the hotly contested U.S. Senate race in Texas.

Meanwhile, Republican Gov. Greg Abbott leads his Democratic challenger, state Rep. Gina Hinojosa, 45% to 40%.

But the issue uniting Texans is their opposition to data centers: 57% said they oppose building a data center in their community, while 30% expressed support.

Here's a deep look at what the poll says on each topic.

The poll was conducted among 1,200 self-reported registered voters between Aug. 5 and 13 and has a margin of error of plus or minus 2.83 percentage points or 3.47% adjusted for weighting.

In a previous Texas Politics Project poll in June, Paxton led Talarico by a percentage point within the poll's margin of error, 43% to 42%, with 84% of Republicans saying they would support Paxton if the election were held then.

The August poll shows that Talarico leads within the poll's margin at 42%, with Paxton at 39%, Libertarian Ted Brown at 3% and 14% expressing no preference.

Talarico is consolidating Democratic support at 91%, while 79% of Republicans have expressed their commitment to Paxton. Among independents, 37% prefer Talarico, 11% prefer Paxton, and 43% express no preference.

Previous polling showed movement toward Democrats, but the Texas Politics Project August poll shows the trend has reversed.

Abbott leads Hinojosa, 45% to 40%, with the remaining 3% preferring Libertarian Pat Dixon, 2% choosing an unspecified "someone else," and 10% unable to express an opinion.

Hinojosa is still keeping the race in the single digits, closer than Democrat Beto O'Rourke's final 11-point loss to Abbott in 2022.

Republican Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick (42%) leads Democratic state Rep. Vikki Goodwin (35%) by seven points.

Republican Attorney General state Sen. Mayes Middleton (40%) leads Democratic state Sen. Nathan Johnson (35%) by five points.

Republican Comptroller Don Huffines (40%) leads Democratic state Sen. Sarah Eckhardt (34%) by six points.

A majority of Texans, 57%, said they oppose building a data center in their community, while only 30% expressed support and 14% had no opinion, according to the Texas Politics Project August poll.

This is the second consecutive poll from the Texas Politics Project to report the same findings, as its June poll showed 29% supported and 56% opposed local data center construction.

Breaking it down by political party,

Republicans remain closely divided: 45% support, 43% oppose.

Democrats strongly oppose: 75% oppose — with 59% saying they strongly oppose, 15% support.

Independents oppose: 54% oppose, 19% support.

Among rural voters, 25% expressed support, while 60% opposed — with 44% strongly opposing the construction of data centers. Suburban Texans mirror the same feelings.

Mateo Rosiles is the Texas Connect reporter for USA TODAY and its regional papers in Texas. Got a news tip for him? Email him at mrosiles@usatodayco.com.
